extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners (applicants and their attorneys), USPTO examining attorneys, and TTAB practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what evidence may be submitted, when remands for additional evidence are appropriate, and how the TTAB treats various kinds of evidence in ex parte trademark appeals and remands to examining attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause for remand for additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of circumstances constituting 'good cause' to suspend and remand an appealed application for additional evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included examples: (1) evidence was not previously available (but not if merely cumulative); (2) a new attorney (transfer from in-house counsel to an outside firm, or assignment to a different examining attorney) takes over and wishes to supplement the record (transfer within the same firm does not by itself constitute good cause); (3) applicant and examining attorney agree to remand. Consent agreements offered in response to a §2(d) refusal are inherently difficult/time-consuming and the Board will grant a request to suspend and remand for consideration of a consent agreement if filed with the Board before the Board's final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on using subsequent publications that are cumulative
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly available evidence may be denied if it is merely cumulative of prior record materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examining attorney's request to remand to submit an article published after filing of the appeal may be denied if the article is substantially the same as articles previously of record; subsequent publication of a single article cannot be used to make of record articles previously available. There is a point where prosecution/examination must end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding party may submit responsive evidence after remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If a remand for additional evidence is granted, the nonrequesting party may submit additional evidence in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on appeal stage, the Board may direct that responsive evidence be submitted with a supplemental brief. If the examining attorney issues a new action on remand, the applicant may have opportunity to submit responsive evidence and, if applicant's appeal brief was already filed, to file a supplemental brief directed to the new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining attorney's permitted actions upon remand for additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: What the examining attorney may do after remand for consideration of new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon remand the examining attorney may approve the application for publication/registration, adhere to the action from which the appeal was taken, or issue a new nonfinal action asserting any new refusal or requirement necessitated by the new evidence. The examining attorney may not assert a new refusal or requirement unrelated to the new evidence unless a 37 CFR §2.142(f)(6) request to remand to assert the new refusal is filed and granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board procedure when examining attorney requests remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Board will allow time for the examining attorney to issue an Office action relating to the new evidence and resume proceedings thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an examining attorney's request to suspend and remand is granted, the Board will allow time to issue an Office action (with no six-month response clause) related to the new evidence; after the new action the application is returned to the Board and proceedings resume. If the examining attorney adheres to or issues a final refusal after remand, omit the six-month response clause and return the application to the Board for resumption of proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of untimely evidence due to actions of nonoffering party
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence submitted after appeal may be considered if the nonoffering party does not object and treats it as of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nonoffering party neither objects to untimely evidence nor avoids discussing it (i.e., affirmatively treats it as part of the record), the Board may consider the evidence. In such cases the Board may permit the opposing party to submit rebuttal evidence. See TBMP §1207.03 examples and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making third-party registrations of record
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party registrations should be submitted as copies or electronic equivalents; mere listings are insufficient to make registrations of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To properly make third‑party registrations of record, submit copies of the registrations themselves or the electronic equivalent from USPTO databases. Mere lists or private search reports are not sufficient. Limited exceptions: if applicant provided a listing during prosecution and the examining attorney failed to advise that the listing was insufficient at a time the applicant could cure, the examining attorney is deemed to have waived objection to the listing (see TBMP §1207.03 and §1208.02). If an examining attorney discusses registrations without objecting, they may be treated as stipulated into the record, but the Board will not consider more than the information actually provided by the applicant (lists of numbers/marks have very limited probative value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence filed with a timely request for reconsideration treated as part of the record
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely request for reconsideration of an appealed action may be accompanied by additional evidence that will be part of the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence filed during the six‑month response period (timely request for reconsideration) is treated as filed prior to appeal even if the notice of appeal was filed earlier in that period. The examining attorney may submit evidence with the response to the request; the applicant may not submit additional evidence in response to examining attorney submissions unless the examining attorney's action is a nonfinal action to which a response may be filed. If a request for reconsideration is denied after a notice of appeal, a subsequent request for reconsideration will be treated as a request for remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of evidence upon remand for new refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional evidence may be submitted when the Board remands for a newly identified issue and the examining attorney issues a new refusal or requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an appealed application is remanded under 37 CFR §2.142(f)(1) (sua sponte remand by the Board) or §2.142(f)(6) (remand on written request by examining attorney) and the examining attorney issues a new refusal or requirement on remand, both the examining attorney and applicant may submit additional evidence. If no new refusal/requirement is made and the application is instead returned to the Board, no additional evidence may be submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter of protest procedure and evidentiary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A third party may file a 'letter of protest' with facts and supporting evidence, and the Deputy Commissioner decides whether to forward it to the examining attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If material from a letter of protest is included in an examining attorney's Office action, that material becomes part of the record for appeal. If the examining attorney wishes to rely on the letter's evidence to support a refusal, the examining attorney must file a 37 CFR §2.142(d) request to suspend and remand (with the additional evidence and a showing of good cause) prior to the Board's final decision. Evidentiary value of letter-of-protest material depends on authentication/foundation and identification of nature or source.

rubrics_metrics.name: More permissive evidentiary approach in ex parte proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board generally tolerates relaxed technical evidentiary requirements in ex parte proceedings, focusing on the spirit and essence of evidence rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there is no cross-examination in ex parte proceedings, the Board is somewhat more lenient (e.g., in consideration of surveys). Affidavits or 37 CFR §2.20 declarations are an established method for introducing evidence in ex parte cases; in inter partes proceedings such affidavits/declarations are not admissible except by agreement of the parties. It remains better practice to present sales figures and similar evidence by affidavit/declaration, though counsel representations may be accepted in certain circumstances (particularly where uncontradicted and not objected to).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value of form declarations and counsel-drafted statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Form declarations and attorney-assisted consumer statements can have probative value but may be viewed skeptically depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has accepted form declarations and attorney-prepared statements where appropriate; identical wording in many declarations 'does not eliminate all value.' However, large numbers of form or virtually identical declarations may be given little weight if contradicted by the record or lacking basic background about declarants. Conclusory statements without evidentiary support are insufficient. The Board's treatment depends on factors such as preparation by counsel, number of form declarations, contradictions in the record, and whether declarants provide background information about their experience with the mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and probative value of NEXIS/database and publication articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles/excerpts from periodicals, NEXIS, and similar databases are evidence of how a term/mark may be perceived, not of the truth of the article's assertions; probative value varies by source and exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newswire stories may have minimal probative value when it's unclear that the story was published in outlets available to consumers; they may be persuasive when there is reason to believe relevant consumers were exposed. Foreign publications are evaluated case-by-case with regard to U.S. consumer exposure. Do not submit all retrieved articles if cumulative or not probative. If submitting a sample, it should be representative of the articles retrieved; submitting only a few without indicating representativeness may lead the Board to assume those are the only supporting articles. If an excerpt is submitted, the nonoffering party may submit the complete article (even after appeal), and submission of full printouts after appeal of articles revealed in an examining attorney's search but not introduced by the examining attorney is generally untimely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's practice on judicial notice of third-party registrations during appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board typically will not take judicial notice of third-party registrations when requested during an appeal; the appeal record must be complete prior to filing of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR §2.142(d) requires the appeal record be complete before filing the appeal; allowing additions during appeal would subvert the rule. Therefore, to make a third-party registration of record, submit a copy (paper USPTO record or electronic record) during prosecution/examination. The Board may exercise discretion in limited circumstances (e.g., Federal Circuit in In re Chippendales), but the established practice is not to take such notice during the appeal.
